newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada consumer holiday spending seen higher.
newsitem.headline: Canada consumer holiday spending seen higher.

text.p: Canadian consumers are likely to open their wallets a little wider this holiday season than last year, said a survey by accounting firm Deloitte & Touche.
"People always underestimate how much they'll spend," Brent Houlden, a partner in Deloitte & Touche's retail group, said. "I was surprised as to how buoyant it was."

The nationwide survey, completed in early September by the Gallup organization, found 49.5 percent of Canadians would spend the same amount this holiday season, while 23.5 percent said they would spend more and 21.6 percent spend less.

However, last year's dismal showing was due to political concerns and a sluggish economy, analysts have said. Quebec's narrowly defeated referendum on separating from Canada on October 30 helped create uncertainty, providing retailers with one of the worst sales seasons ever.
Despite consumer optimism, "it's still not going to be a great Christmas this year," Houlden said.

The recent bankruptcy of showroom catalogue retailer Consumers Distributing, with 216 stores across Canada, will depress the profits of other retailers as its stock is sold off at discount prices between now and year-end, Houlden said.
"That will steal Christmas from the other retailers," Houlden said.
Houlden added that he would not be surprised if another retailer went bankrupt within the next few weeks, temporarily reducing profit margins further for surviving firms.

The Gallup survey also broke down responses by income, occupation and mother tongue, Deloitte & Touche said. Consumers with lower incomes tend to anticipate more holiday season spending this year as a treat to themselves, while higher income earners like to splurge year-round, Houlden said.
Housewives like to wrap up holiday shopping well before the season hits, while men and students seem to wait until the last minute, Houlden said.

The survey also found differences between native French and English speakers. About 59.3 percent of respondents whose mother tongue is French expected to spend the same amount this year, compared to 48.1 percent of English speakers.
Another 20 percent of native French-speakers said they would spend more, while 15.2 percent foresaw lower expenditures, the survey showed.
This compared to 22.5 percent of English-speakers who said they would increase spending while 24.2 percent saw less expenditure.
"There's definitely an opportunity here for retailers to tailor their advertising," Houlden said.
Gallup surveyed 1,231 Canadians and the survey is considered accurate within 2.9 percent, 19 times out of 20.
